e.etymology: A spelling of Suzanne, the French form of Susanna, from Hebrew Shoshannah, 'lily'.
A feminine elaboration of Verna or Vernon with the Spanish-style ending -ita, used in the US in the mid-1900s.
A pet form of Susan or Susanna used in the American South in the 1800s. Susanna comes from Hebrew Shoshannah, 'lily'.
A feminine form of Cletus, which is short for Anacletus, from Greek anakletos, 'called upon'. An early pope bore the name.
A short form of Latoya, an American name that La Toya Jackson made widely known.
An American name of the 1970s, close in sound to Nakia and Nikita and to Nikki, the short form of Nicole.
A respelling of Jeffrey, the medieval English form of Geoffrey, which the Normans brought over. Its second part is Germanic frid, 'peace'; the first part is disputed.
A respelling of Jacqueline, the French feminine of Jacques, the French form of James and Jacob. Jacob is traditionally explained as 'holder of the heel' or 'supplanter'.
A spelling of Lavinia from the American South. In Virgil's Aeneid, Lavinia is the princess Aeneas marries, and the name is older than Latin, with no known meaning.
A spelling of Corinne, the French form of Corinna, from Greek kore, 'maiden'. Corinna was an ancient Greek poet.
A respelling of Tabitha, Aramaic for 'gazelle'. In the Acts of the Apostles, Tabitha (Dorcas in Greek) is a charitable woman whom Peter raises from the dead.
A nickname turned given name, from the color pink or the garden flower called a pink. It was most used for girls in the American South around 1900.

assoc.t: pinkie, the everyday word for the little finger
Pinkie Pie, the pink pony in My Little Pony

e.etymology: An African American name of the 1970s built with the Ta- prefix, in a family with Tawana and Tawanda; the ending echoes Wanda and Juana.
A respelling of Yolanda, the Spanish form of the medieval French name Yolande, which is probably a form of Violante, from Latin viola, 'violet'.
A phonetic American spelling of Cherie, from French chérie, 'darling'.
A feminine form of William, used in the American South around 1900, often to name a daughter after her father. William comes from Germanic wil, 'will', and helm, 'helmet, protection'.
The short form of Barbara, from Greek barbaros, 'foreign'. St. Barbara made the name one of the most used in Christian Europe.
e.note: A barb is also a sharp point or a cutting remark.

e.etymology: From a Cornish surname taken from the manor of Denzell in Cornwall. It passed into English use as a first name in the 1600s, and Denzel is the same name.
A respelling of Debbie, the pet form of Deborah, Hebrew for 'bee'. In the Bible Deborah is a prophetess and judge of Israel.
A respelling of Megan, a Welsh pet form of Meg, short for Margaret, from Greek margarites, 'pearl'. The -gh- spellings arose outside Wales on the look of Irish names.
A respelling of Jared, from Hebrew Yered, 'descent'. In Genesis Jared is the father of Enoch and lives 962 years.
A short form of Margaret and Marjorie, from Greek margarites, 'pearl'.

assoc.t: Marge Simpson, the mother on The Simpsons

e.etymology: An American name of the 1970s that puts a T- on Angela, in line with Tammy and Tanya. Angela comes from Greek angelos, 'messenger'.
A respelling of Sharon, the Hebrew name of the fertile coastal plain of Israel, praised in the Song of Songs for its flowers. Sharon became a girls' name in the 20th century.
A respelling of Sharon, the Hebrew name of the fertile coastal plain of Israel, praised in the Song of Songs for its flowers. Sharon became a girls' name in the 20th century.
A feminine form of Thomas, in use in England since the Middle Ages. Thomas comes from Aramaic te'oma, 'twin'.
In the US, an elaboration of Laverne or of Verna with the La- prefix. It happens to match Laverna, the Roman goddess of thieves.
From an English surname of uncertain origin that became a first name in the American South in the 1800s.
An American name of the 1930s and 40s, most likely a variant of Galen, the name of the ancient Greek physician, from galene, 'calm'.
A spelling of Phyllis, Greek for 'foliage'. In Greek myth Phyllis dies of love and becomes an almond tree. This is the spelling of the poet Phillis Wheatley.
namesakes: Phillis Wheatley (first published African American poet)

e.etymology: A respelling of Debra, the streamlined American form of Deborah, Hebrew for 'bee'. In the Bible Deborah is a prophetess and judge of Israel.
A spelling of Tamika, an American name of the 1960s and 70s thought to come from Japanese Tamiko, which reached US audiences through the 1962 film A Girl Named Tamiko.
